title: Use const by default, let when it changes
why_it_matters: Readers see at a glance what can change.
explanation: Start every variable with const. Switch to let only when you need to assign a new value later, like a counter. This makes the code easier to read, because a const name always points to the same value.
try_it: Change every var in an old script to const, and use let only where the code breaks.

title: const does not freeze what it holds
why_it_matters: It clears up the most common const confusion.
explanation: const stops you from reassigning the variable, not from changing what it holds. You can push to a const array or edit the properties of a const object. Reassigning with = is what throws a TypeError.
try_it: Declare a const array, push two items into it, then try to reassign it.

title: Avoid var in new code
why_it_matters: var leaks out of blocks and causes odd bugs.
explanation: var is scoped to the whole function, not to the nearest braces, so a loop variable stays alive after the loop. let and const are scoped to their block, which is safer and easier to reason about.
try_it: Run this code and read the error you get when you log j.

title: let and const live inside their braces
why_it_matters: You know where a variable can and cannot be used.
explanation: A variable declared with let or const inside curly braces exists only in that block. Code outside the braces cannot see it and throws a ReferenceError. Declare a variable in the outer block if you need it later.
try_it: Move the declaration out of the if block so the log works.

title: Hoisting: var is undefined, let throws
why_it_matters: It explains two very different error messages.
explanation: Declarations are registered before the code runs. A var is available early with the value undefined. let and const exist too, but sit in a temporal dead zone until their line runs, so reading them early throws.
try_it: Run it and compare the first log with the second error.

title: Quiz: what does typeof null return?
why_it_matters: It is a famous trap in interviews and real code.
explanation: Question: what does typeof null return? Answer: "object". This is an old bug kept for compatibility. Check for null with === null instead. Arrays also report "object", so use Array.isArray for them.
code:
console.log(typeof null); // "object"
console.log(typeof undefined); // "undefined"
console.log(typeof []); // "object"
try_it: Log typeof for a string, a number, null and an array.

title: JavaScript has seven primitive types
why_it_matters: Knowing them shows what typeof can tell you.
explanation: The primitives are string, number, bigint, boolean, undefined, null and symbol. Everything else is an object, including arrays and functions. Primitives are immutable values, which behave differently from objects when copied.
try_it: Write one example value for each of the seven primitives.

title: Primitives are copied, objects are shared
why_it_matters: It explains why changing one object changes another.
explanation: Assigning a primitive copies its value. Assigning an object copies the reference, so both names point to the same object. Changing it through one name is visible through the other.
try_it: Predict the values of a and x.n, then run the code to check.

title: Use === instead of ==
why_it_matters: Strict equality never converts types behind your back.
explanation: === compares value and type, so 5 === "5" is false. == converts types first, which gives surprising results. Use === everywhere unless you have a specific reason not to.
code:
console.log(5 === "5"); // false
console.log(5 == "5"); // true
try_it: Search your code for == and replace each one with ===.

title: Why == gives surprising answers
why_it_matters: It shows the type coercion that === avoids.
explanation: The loose == operator converts values to a common type before comparing, using rules that are hard to remember. An empty string equals 0, and null equals undefined, but null does not equal 0.
code:
console.log(0 == ""); // true
console.log("1" == 1); // true
console.log(null == undefined); // true
console.log(null == 0); // false
try_it: Predict each result before running the code, then count how many you got right.

title: Quiz: what are "5" + 3 and "5" - 3?
why_it_matters: The plus sign behaves differently from minus.
explanation: Question: what do "5" + 3 and "5" - 3 give? Answer: "53" and 2. With a string, + joins text, but - only works on numbers, so JavaScript converts "5" to a number first.
code:
console.log("5" + 3); // "53"
console.log("5" - 3); // 2
try_it: Convert a string with Number() before adding to avoid the join.

title: The falsy values you should memorize
why_it_matters: Conditions use them every day.
explanation: These values count as false in a condition: false, 0, an empty string, null, undefined and NaN. Almost everything else is truthy. Knowing the list helps you read if statements correctly.
try_it: Test each falsy value with an if statement.

title: Myth: an empty array is falsy
why_it_matters: It stops a classic condition bug.
explanation: Myth: an empty array counts as false. Arrays and objects are always truthy, even when empty. To check whether an array has items, test its length instead of the array itself.
try_it: Write an if that prints a message only when an array has items.

title: ?? keeps 0 and empty strings
why_it_matters: Defaults no longer overwrite valid falsy values.
explanation: The || operator replaces any falsy value, so a count of 0 becomes your default. The ?? operator replaces only null and undefined. Use ?? when 0, false or an empty string are valid values.
try_it: Find a default made with || in your code and decide whether ?? is safer.

title: Optional chaining stops crashes
why_it_matters: Missing data no longer throws a TypeError.
explanation: Reading a property of undefined throws an error. The ?. operator stops and returns undefined instead when the value before it is null or undefined. It is perfect for data that may not exist yet.
try_it: Read a deeply nested property from an empty object using ?.

title: NaN is not equal to itself
why_it_matters: You need the right tool to detect it.
explanation: NaN means not a number, and it is the only value in JavaScript that is not equal to itself. NaN === NaN is false. Use Number.isNaN() to check for it. Failed conversions like Number("abc") produce it.
code:
console.log(NaN === NaN); // false
console.log(Number.isNaN(NaN)); // true
console.log(Number("abc")); // NaN
try_it: Convert "abc" to a number and check the result with Number.isNaN.

title: Common mistake: switch without break
why_it_matters: Cases fall through and run extra code.
explanation: Inside a switch, execution continues into the next case unless you stop it with break. Forgetting break makes several cases run. Add break at the end of each case, or return from the function.
try_it: Remove one break and see which extra line runs.

title: for...of loops over values, for...in over keys
why_it_matters: Mixing them up gives indexes instead of items.
explanation: for...of gives you each value of an array or other iterable. for...in gives the property names, which for an array are the indexes as strings. Use for...of for arrays and for...in only for objects.
try_it: Loop over an array with both and compare what each prints.

title: Common mistake: the off-by-one loop
why_it_matters: It causes undefined values at the end of a loop.
explanation: Array indexes start at 0, so the last valid index is length minus 1. Using <= with length runs one time too many and reads undefined. Use < arr.length as the condition.
try_it: Log arr[i] in the buggy loop and find the undefined.

title: Common mistake: = instead of ===
why_it_matters: A single character turns a test into an assignment.
explanation: Writing = inside an if assigns a value instead of comparing, and the condition then uses the assigned value. With a truthy number it always runs. Use === to compare.
try_it: Run the code and check the value of x afterward.

title: The ternary operator for simple choices
why_it_matters: It turns a small if/else into one readable line.
explanation: The ternary operator is condition ? valueIfTrue : valueIfFalse. It is best for choosing between two values. For longer logic, a regular if statement is clearer, and nested ternaries are hard to read.
code:
const age = 20;
const label = age >= 18 ? "adult" : "minor";
try_it: Rewrite a small if/else that sets one variable as a ternary.

title: Shadowing: same name, different scope
why_it_matters: It explains why a value seems to change or not.
explanation: A variable declared in an inner scope can reuse the name of an outer one. Inside, the inner one hides the outer one, and the outer value stays untouched. It is legal but can confuse readers, so avoid it.
try_it: Rename the inner variable and see the code become clearer.

title: Common mistake: a typo creates a global
why_it_matters: Silent globals hide bugs until much later.
explanation: In sloppy mode, assigning to a name you never declared silently creates a global variable. Adding "use strict" turns it into a ReferenceError. Modules and classes are strict by default.
try_it: Remove "use strict" and check whether total becomes a global.

title: Project idea: a tip calculator
why_it_matters: It uses variables, numbers and conditions together.
explanation: Build a tip calculator that takes a bill amount and a tip percentage, then shows the tip and the total. Add a rule for a default tip when the field is empty, and validate that the bill is a positive number.
try_it: Write the formula on paper for a 20 dollar bill and a 15 percent tip.

title: Project idea: a number guessing game
why_it_matters: It practices loops, conditions and comparisons.
explanation: Pick a random number between 1 and 100 and let the player guess. After each guess say higher, lower or correct, and count the attempts. Stop the game after ten tries and show the answer.
try_it: List the three outcomes of a guess before you write any code.
